why: The old solution breaks off mid-algebra and asserts the answer; worked through, the tower height is \(h\cos 2\theta\) (option C), not the keyed \(h\cos\theta\). With tower \(T\) at distance \(d\): \(T=d\tan\theta\) and \(h=d(\tan 2\theta-\tan\theta)=d\sin\theta/(\cos\theta\cos 2\theta)\), so \(T/h=\cos 2\theta\). At \(\theta=30^\circ\), \(d=1\): \(T=0.5774\), \(h=1.1547\), \(h\cos 2\theta=0.5774\) while \(h\cos\theta=1.0000\). Either the key should be C or the stem's angles are mislabelled.

With the exponent \(4/3\) given in the stem, cubing both sides yields \(\left[1+(y')^2\right]^3=(y'')^4\), so the highest-order derivative carries power 4 and the degree is 4 (option D), not the keyed 3. Degree 3 follows only from the mirror-image stem \(1+(y')^2=(y'')^{3/4}\), which on raising to the 4th power gives \(\left[1+(y')^2\right]^4=(y'')^3\). So either the stem exponent is transposed or the key is wrong; the old solution's closing sentence contradicts its own first line.

\(f'(x)=-m/x^2+2n\) and \(f'(2)=0\) give \(-m/4+2n=0\), i.e. \(m=8n\). That fixes \(m-8n=0\) but leaves \(m+8n=16n\) undetermined, so the stem as given supports option D, not the keyed 0. Option B requires the stem to ask for \(m-8n\), or the function to read \(f(x)=m/x-2nx+1\) (which gives \(m=-8n\) and \(m+8n=0\)). The existing solution already reaches this conclusion correctly but presents it as a key/stem disagreement rather than a derivation; it needs a source check, not a rewrite.
The old solution described the permutation loosely and then leaned on a numerical spot-check; the sign is now obtained by counting interchanges explicitly.
solution:
A determinant is unchanged by transposition, so transpose first:
\(\begin{vmatrix} a_{21} & a_{31} & a_{11} \\ a_{23} & a_{33} & a_{13} \\ a_{22} & a_{32} & a_{12} \end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix} a_{21} & a_{23} & a_{22} \\ a_{31} & a_{33} & a_{32} \\ a_{11} & a_{13} & a_{12} \end{vmatrix}\)

Read the transposed array against \(A\). Its three rows are rows 2, 3, 1 of \(A\), and within every row the columns stand in the order 1, 3, 2. So it is \(A\) with one row rearrangement and one column rearrangement.

Rows: to go from the order \((1,2,3)\) to \((2,3,1)\), interchange \(R_1\leftrightarrow R_2\) to get \((2,1,3)\), then \(R_2\leftrightarrow R_3\) to get \((2,3,1)\). Two interchanges contribute \((-1)^2=+1\).

Columns: the order \((1,3,2)\) comes from \((1,2,3)\) by the single interchange \(C_2\leftrightarrow C_3\), contributing \(-1\).

Therefore the determinant equals \((+1)(-1)\Delta=-\Delta\).

Hence (D).

why: The old solution quoted \(I_2=\pi/\sqrt{2}\) without proof and asserted \(I_1=\frac{\pi}{2}I_2\); both steps are now derived.
solution:
Step 1 — strip the \(x\) out of \(I_1\). Apply \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx=\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx\) with \(a=\pi\), using \(\cos^2(\pi-x)=\cos^2x\):
\(I_1=\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{\pi-x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx\).
Add this to the original expression for \(I_1\):
\(2I_1=\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{\pi}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx\), so \(I_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2}J\) where \(J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{dx}{1+\cos^2x}\).

Step 2 — evaluate \(J\). Since \(\cos^2(\pi-x)=\cos^2x\), the integrand is symmetric about \(x=\pi/2\), so \(J=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\cos^2x}\). Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^2x\) and use \(\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x\):
\(J=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\sec^2x+1}\,dx=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x}{2+\tan^2x}\,dx\).
Put \(t=\tan x\), \(dt=\sec^2x\,dx\); as \(x:0\to\pi/2\), \(t:0\to\infty\):
\(J=2\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{dt}{2+t^2}=2\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{\sqrt2}\right]_0^{\infty}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt2}\).

Step 3 — combine. \(I_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\pi^2}{2\sqrt2}\), so \(I_1^2=\dfrac{\pi^4}{4\cdot2}=\dfrac{\pi^4}{8}\) and \(8I_1^2=\pi^4\).

Hence (D).

why: The old solution quoted the value of the integral outright; the substitution that produces it is now shown.
solution:
Because \(\sin^2(\pi-x)=\sin^2x\), the integrand is symmetric about \(x=\pi/2\), so
\(I_2=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\sin^2x}\).

Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^2x\), and use \(\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x\) so that \(\sec^2x+\tan^2x=1+2\tan^2x\):
\(I_2=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\sec^2x+\tan^2x}\,dx=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x}{1+2\tan^2x}\,dx\).

Put \(t=\tan x\), so \(dt=\sec^2x\,dx\) and the limits \(x:0\to\pi/2\) become \(t:0\to\infty\):
\(I_2=2\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{dt}{1+2t^2}=2\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt2\,t\right)\right]_0^{\infty}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt2}\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution mis-stated the rationalisation, left a surd expansion unfinished and closed with a numerical check; the product is now factorised into perfect squares so the root is exact.
solution:
For \((3+2\sqrt2)x^2-(4+2\sqrt3)x+(8+4\sqrt3)=0\), the product of the roots is
\(\alpha\beta=\dfrac{8+4\sqrt3}{3+2\sqrt2}\), and the GM is \(\sqrt{\alpha\beta}\).

Write both parts as perfect squares:
\(8+4\sqrt3=2\left(4+2\sqrt3\right)=2\left(\sqrt3+1\right)^2\), since \(\left(\sqrt3+1\right)^2=3+2\sqrt3+1=4+2\sqrt3\);
\(3+2\sqrt2=\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^2\), since \(\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^2=2+2\sqrt2+1=3+2\sqrt2\).

So \(\alpha\beta=\dfrac{2\left(\sqrt3+1\right)^2}{\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^2}\) and
\(\text{GM}=\sqrt{\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{\sqrt2\left(\sqrt3+1\right)}{\sqrt2+1}\).

Rationalise the denominator: \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2+1}=\dfrac{\sqrt2-1}{(\sqrt2+1)(\sqrt2-1)}=\sqrt2-1\). Hence
\(\text{GM}=\sqrt2\left(\sqrt3+1\right)\left(\sqrt2-1\right)\).

Expand the bracket product: \(\left(\sqrt3+1\right)\left(\sqrt2-1\right)=\sqrt6-\sqrt3+\sqrt2-1\), so
\(\text{GM}=\sqrt2\left(\sqrt6-\sqrt3+\sqrt2-1\right)\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution jumped from the substitution to a quadratic in \(s\) that does not follow, then quoted a root; the elimination between \(s\) and \(\sin 2x\) is now carried out in full.
solution:
Put \(s=\sin x+\cos x\) and \(S=\sin 2x=2\sin x\cos x\). Squaring \(s\) gives \(s^2=1+2\sin x\cos x=1+S\), and \(\sin x\cos x=\dfrac{S}{2}\).

Collect the four reciprocal terms over \(\sin x\cos x\):
\(\tan x+\cot x=\dfrac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}=\dfrac{1}{\sin x\cos x}=\dfrac{2}{S}\),
\(\sec x+\operatorname{cosec} x=\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}=\dfrac{2s}{S}\).

The given equation becomes \(s+\dfrac{2}{S}+\dfrac{2s}{S}=7\). Multiply through by \(S\), which is legitimate since \(S=\sin 2x=0\) would leave \(\tan x,\cot x,\sec x,\operatorname{cosec} x\) undefined:
\(sS+2+2s=7S\Rightarrow s(S+2)=7S-2\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{7S-2}{S+2}\).

Now eliminate \(s\) using \(s^2=1+S\):
\((7S-2)^2=(1+S)(S+2)^2\).
Left side: \(49S^2-28S+4\).
Right side: \((1+S)(S^2+4S+4)=S^2+4S+4+S^3+4S^2+4S=S^3+5S^2+8S+4\).
Subtracting,
\(S^3+5S^2+8S+4-49S^2+28S-4=0\Rightarrow S^3-44S^2+36S=0\Rightarrow S\left(S^2-44S+36\right)=0\).

Discarding \(S=0\), the equation reduces to \(\sin^2 2x-44\sin 2x+36=0\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution skipped the equal-tangent step and quoted a quadratic \(m^2-16m-36=0\) that does not come from its own cosine-rule line; the algebra is now done and it factors far more simply.
solution:
The two tangents drawn to a circle from an external point are equal, so at each vertex the two touch-lengths agree:
\(PN=PM=n\), \(QL=QN=n+2\), \(RM=RL=n+4\).

Therefore
\(PQ=PN+NQ=n+(n+2)=2n+2\),
\(PR=PM+MR=n+(n+4)=2n+4\),
\(QR=QL+LR=(n+2)+(n+4)=2n+6\).

Apply the cosine rule at \(P\), the angle opposite \(QR\):
\(\cos P=\dfrac{PQ^2+PR^2-QR^2}{2\cdot PQ\cdot PR}\).

Numerator: \((2n+2)^2+(2n+4)^2-(2n+6)^2=(4n^2+8n+4)+(4n^2+16n+16)-(4n^2+24n+36)=4n^2-16=4(n-2)(n+2)\).
Denominator: \(2(2n+2)(2n+4)=2\cdot2(n+1)\cdot2(n+2)=8(n+1)(n+2)\).

So \(\cos P=\dfrac{4(n-2)(n+2)}{8(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac{n-2}{2(n+1)}\).

Set this equal to \(\dfrac13\):
\(3(n-2)=2(n+1)\Rightarrow 3n-6=2n+2\Rightarrow n=8\).

The sides are then \(18,20,22\), and \(\cos P=\dfrac{18^2+20^2-22^2}{2(18)(20)}=\dfrac{240}{720}=\dfrac13\); \(QR=22\) is the longest side, so \(P\) is indeed the largest angle, as the question requires.

Hence (C).

why: The old solution stalled at \(A=\pi/2\) (a wrong deduction) and then quoted the answer; the condition in fact reduces to \(A=|B-C|\), and the branch giving a determinate value is identified explicitly.
solution:
First simplify what is asked:
\(\tan\dfrac B2+\cot\dfrac B2=\dfrac{\sin^2(B/2)+\cos^2(B/2)}{\sin(B/2)\cos(B/2)}=\dfrac{1}{\tfrac12\sin B}=\dfrac{2}{\sin B}\).

Now use the given condition. Since \(A+B+C=\pi\), we have \(\dfrac{B+C}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac A2\), so \(\cos\dfrac{B+C}{2}=\sin\dfrac A2\) and
\(\cos B+\cos C=2\cos\dfrac{B+C}{2}\cos\dfrac{B-C}{2}=2\sin\dfrac A2\cos\dfrac{B-C}{2}\),
while \(\sin A=2\sin\dfrac A2\cos\dfrac A2\).

Equating the two sides of \(\sin A=\cos B+\cos C\) and cancelling \(\sin\dfrac A2\), which is non-zero for \(0<A<\pi\):
\(\cos\dfrac A2=\cos\dfrac{B-C}{2}\).
Both \(\dfrac A2\) and \(\dfrac{B-C}{2}\) lie in \(\left(-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right)\), where cosine is one-to-one on magnitudes, so \(A=|B-C|\).

Take \(A=B-C\). Then \(B=A+C\), and substituting into \(A+B+C=\pi\) gives \(B+B=\pi\), so \(B=\dfrac\pi2\) and \(\sin B=1\). Therefore
\(\tan\dfrac B2+\cot\dfrac B2=\dfrac{2}{\sin B}=2\).

Hence (D).

[Note on the other branch: \(A=C-B\) forces \(C=\dfrac\pi2\) and leaves \(B\) free, so \(2/\sin B\) is then not a fixed number and matches none of the four options (for example \(A=60^\circ,B=30^\circ,C=90^\circ\) satisfies the given condition and gives \(4\)). The configuration intended by the question is the right angle at \(B\).]

why: The old solution asserted the two component integrals equal \(\pi/4\); the pairing argument that establishes it is now shown.
solution:
Split the numerator and write
\(J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\), \(\;K=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\), so that \(k=\dfrac{aJ+bK}{a+b}\).

Adding the two integrals:
\(J+K=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}dx=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

The two are also equal. Apply \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx=\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx\) to \(J\) with \(a=\dfrac\pi2\), using \(\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\cos x\) and \(\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\sin x\):
\(J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x+\sin x}\,dx=K\).

So \(2J=\dfrac\pi2\), giving \(J=K=\dfrac\pi4\), and therefore
\(k=\dfrac{a\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}+b\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}}{a+b}=\dfrac{(a+b)\frac{\pi}{4}}{a+b}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution wandered through fractional powers and a special case before stumbling onto the answer; parametrising the GP by its common ratio settles it in two lines.
solution:
Let the common ratio of the GP \(p,\;g_1,\;g_2,\;q\) be \(r\). Then
\(g_1=pr\), \(g_2=pr^2\), \(q=pr^3\).

So
\(\dfrac{g_1^2}{g_2}=\dfrac{p^2r^2}{pr^2}=p\), and \(\dfrac{g_2^2}{g_1}=\dfrac{p^2r^4}{pr}=pr^3=q\).

Adding, \(\dfrac{g_1^2}{g_2}+\dfrac{g_2^2}{g_1}=p+q\).

Since \(m\) is the arithmetic mean of \(p\) and \(q\), \(m=\dfrac{p+q}{2}\), so \(p+q=2m\).

Hence (B).

why: The determinant is expanded term by term to \(q-p+2\), the positivity condition is turned into the exact equivalence \(q+2>p\), and A and B are killed by an explicit counterexample; the bracketed paragraph is an honest record of the genuine C-versus-D option overlap in the paper, not a substitute for a derivation.
The old solution trailed off mid-identity twice and then asserted the value; the numerator and denominator are now each reduced to \(\sin 40^\circ\) so the ratio is exact.
solution:
\(\dfrac{\sqrt3\,p}{4}-\dfrac{q}{4}=\dfrac14\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sin 20^\circ}-\dfrac{1}{\sin 70^\circ}\right)=\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3\sin 70^\circ-\sin 20^\circ}{\sin 20^\circ\sin 70^\circ}\).

Use \(\sin 70^\circ=\cos 20^\circ\) throughout.

Numerator: \(\sqrt3\cos 20^\circ-\sin 20^\circ=2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos 20^\circ-\dfrac12\sin 20^\circ\right)=2\left(\sin 60^\circ\cos 20^\circ-\cos 60^\circ\sin 20^\circ\right)\).
By \(\sin(X-Y)=\sin X\cos Y-\cos X\sin Y\), this is \(2\sin\left(60^\circ-20^\circ\right)=2\sin 40^\circ\).

Denominator: \(\sin 20^\circ\cos 20^\circ=\dfrac12\left(2\sin 20^\circ\cos 20^\circ\right)=\dfrac12\sin 40^\circ\).

Therefore
\(\dfrac{\sqrt3\,p}{4}-\dfrac{q}{4}=\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac{2\sin 40^\circ}{\tfrac12\sin 40^\circ}=\dfrac14\times 4=1\).

Hence (C).
